newsitem.title: USA: US jobs data hint at further Fed hike - Fed alumni.
newsitem.headline: US jobs data hint at further Fed hike - Fed alumni.

text.p: Strong U.S. employment data might have taken Wall Street by surprise last week, but the numbers are probably in line with the Federal Reserve's own forecasts and are supportive of another interest rate hike in May, former Fed officials and economists said.

"These are stronger numbers than most economists ... had forecast, but they may be quite consonant with the Federal Reserve Board's own internal forecast," said Preston Martin, a former Fed vice-chairman.

"(The data) support the action that was already taken at the last Federal Open Market Committee and they point to another action on May 20," added Martin, who is currently the chairman of San Francisco-based HomeVest Financial Services.
Martin expects the Fed to raise the federal funds rate again by another 25 basis points when the central bank's policy-setting body meets next on May 20.
The Fed hiked its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25.
On Friday the Labor Department released its April employment report showing the nation's jobless rate fell to a 23-year low of 4.9 percent versus the 5.2 percent recorded in March.
The number landed on Wall Street together with a 142,000 gain in April non-farm payrolls and a slight one-cent drop in average hourly earnings to $12.14.
Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities and a former Federal Reserve economist, said he believed the April employment report was mixed.

Moran added, however, that weakness seen in certain areas of the report, such as manufacturing and construction employment, are probably temporary and more related to seasonal and weather factors rather than representing an underlying trend.
Thus Moran expects the Fed to raise the federal funds rate again by a quarter of a percentange point to 5.75 percent at the May 20 FOMC meeting.
"As I look at the report, the elements that you would classify as soft elements and weak elements I think are temporary factors or seasonal aberrations," Moran said.
"On the other hand, the key factors suggesting strength, such as drop in the unemployment rate, are accurate indications of underlying trends," Moran added.

Analysts said the employment data suggested the economy might slow down from its red hot first quarter levels but it is still far from cooling to a point where inflationary pressures are no longer a concern.

"These are very strong numbers, there's no real sign of inflation yet, but again they point toward 1998 inflationary tendencies," Martin said, explaining why the Fed has to act now to nip inflation before it sprouts.
Pundits said the same trend was suggested by the slight drop in the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index to 54.2 in April from 55.0 in March.
The U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by a sizzling 5.6 percent in the first quarter of 1997.
Analysts said the Fed's main concern now appears to be the fact that the economy continues to grow rapidly, quickly using up labor supplies without a corresponding increase in productivity.

"The unemployment rate went down a ton. And the Fed has got to be concerned about that fact that the unemployment has gotten down to a point now where wage rate increases are likely to begin moving up further," said Lyle Gramley, a former Federal Reserve Board governor.

"That I think is the Fed's principal concern. The economy has been going so fast that we're straining our supplies of labor resources, and that ultimately may give rise to inflation," added Gramley, currently a consulting economist for the Mortgage Bankers Association.
Gramley said that forecasting the outcome of the May Fed meeting was "a close call," but he added that "it's only a question of when the Fed moves.

"This economy is too strong. They are going to need to tighten monetary policy and raise interest rates to avoid a too strong economic growth pattern continuing that would bring problems on the inflation front."
Gramley said the next key indicator expected to shed more light on that issue is the retail sales report for April, which is scheduled for release on May 13.
